Korhi Average Adjusters & Surveyors have been appointed to handle the adjustment for the 5,593 teu containership, with Korhi and Richards Hogg Lindley responsible for collecting general average security. Those with cargo aboard will be required to provide salvage security and general average security before shipments can be forwarded or released, while uninsured cargo owners will be required to provide cash deposits, although the amounts have yet to be determined. Given the extent of cargo damage and timetable for discharging containers remains unclear, the requirements add more uncertainty for forwarders and their customers with shipments aboard the vessel. items.summary: A new storm of stakeholder disputes, and potential operational disruption, is brewing across Indian ports over policy changes by container lines on empty-container handling and associated depot charges. Maersk, for example, has substantially raised its lift-on/lift-off (lo-lo) charges for empties moving via Mundra, India’s busiest container port and the primary gateway for the hinterlands around Delhi. The revision, implemented from 1 November, effectively more than doubled the rates shippers had been charged, from $23 to $51 per 20ft empty box, and from $31 to $67 per 40ft, plus local taxes. The CCBA claimed the policy shift was fraught with “serious economic and operational implications for cargo agents”, as it had seen third-party vendors keep inflating tariffs once taken over.

items.title: India’s coking coal import dependence on Australia falls to 54%
items.original_title: India’s coking coal import dependence on Australia falls to 54%
items.summary: India’s dependence on Australia for coking coal imports fell to 54% in 2025 from 73% in 2019, according to a deposition by the steel ministry to a parliamentary standing committee. About 90% of India’s coking coal requirement, a key raw material for steelmaking via the BF-BOF route, is met through imports because India has limited availability of high-quality, low-ash coking coal. Australia remains India’s largest source of coking coal imports, but the share of Russia rose from 0.62% to 8.15%, the US from 8% to 17%, Mozambique from 4% to 7.31% and Indonesia from 2.46% to 4%. India’s steel sector imported 58 Mt of coking coal in FY25, up from 57 Mt in FY24, at a cost of around Rs 1.5 lakh crore. Under the Aatmanirbhar Coal Mission, the government’s Mission Coking Coal targets 140 Mt of domestic raw coking coal production by 2030 – 105 Mt from Coal India Limited and 35 Mt from private allocations – while aiming to raise the blending ratio of domestic coal in steelmaking from 10% to 30%. Globally, high-quality hard coking coal is concentrated in a few countries, and Australia accounts for more than 50% of internationally traded coking coal owing to its high-quality reserves, stable mining ecosystem and efficient logistics. items.title: Record supply growth pushes container fleet towards 50m teu by 2030
items.original_title: Record supply growth pushes container fleet towards 50m teu by 2030
items.summary: The global containership fleet is heading towards an unprecedented 50m teu by 2030, setting the stage for a potentially devastating oversupply crisis and enormous downward pressure on freight rates. New analysis from Sea-Intelligence shows the fleet expanding from today’s 34m teu to 40m teu by the second quarter of 2028 and 50m teu by the third quarter of 2030, the largest capacity expansion in container shipping history. Combined with an estimated 8% effective capacity boost from the return of Asia-Europe services to the Suez Canal, cumulative supply growth could exceed 50% by the end of the decade. The consultancy calculates that quarterly newbuilding deliveries will average 1m teu between 2027 and 2030, peaking at an extraordinary 1.8m teu in the third quarter of 2028. Even if carriers repeated the record demolition levels of 2016 every year through 2030, this would absorb less than 17% of incoming capacity, leaving annual fleet growth averaging 8.5%. By 2030, some 10.8m teu will be aboard ships older than 20 years, although Sea-Intelligence doubts carriers intend to scrap anything approaching that figure. The warnings follow a similarly bearish forecast from Xeneta, which expects fleet growth of 6.8% next year against demand growth of just 2.5% to 4%.

The United Nations climate conference begins Monday in Antalya and runs through November 20, with the transition toward cleaner energy among the central issues under discussion. Residents of Ikizkoy, near the Akbelen forest in southwestern Mugla province, want delegates to visit communities affected by decades of lignite mining and the expansion of nearby coal operations. Coal generated 34% of Turkey’s electricity last year, making the country Europe’s largest producer of coal-fired power, according to energy research group Ember. Mining operations around Akbelen supply the Yenikoy and Kemerkoy power plants, which together generate slightly more than 2% of Turkey’s electricity. Turkey is proposing a voluntary global electrification target at COP31, although its climate benefits would depend on whether additional electricity comes from low-carbon sources. Energy Minister Alparslan Bayraktar acknowledged the difficulties of reducing coal dependence, citing thousands of jobs supported by mining operations. Ankara considers nuclear power a major alternative and aims to develop 10 gigawatts of nuclear generation capacity by 2040, roughly equivalent to the country’s current coal-powered output.

items.summary: A wave of tanker deliveries is set to test whether geopolitical disruption and longer trading routes can continue supporting charter rates and ship values, according to S&P Global Energy CERA’s latest fleet outlook, after an extraordinary freight market rally pushed some secondhand ship values above newbuilding order prices. Taking newbuild order books and scrapping into account, CERA analysts forecast global tanker capacity will rise from 703.72 million deadweight tons at the end of 2025 to 743.56 million dwt in 2026, 778.35 million dwt in 2027 and 830.61 million dwt in 2028, before reaching 862.98 million dwt in 2029. That would represent cumulative growth of 22.6% over four years. “The critical issue is not whether supply will grow, it clearly will, but whether ton-mile demand, scrapping, sanctions-related inefficiencies and operational segmentation can absorb that growth without a material decline in utilization and freight rates.” Record rates Tanker rates across segments have risen to record levels following the outbreak of the US-Iran war at the end of February, boosted by increased ship requirements as Asian importers seek barrels from farther afield and Middle Eastern producers rely on ship-to-ship transfers to mitigate transit risks around the Strait of Hormuz. items.title: Finland Sees Continued Demand for Icebreakers Despite Warming Winters, Citing Security Concerns
items.original_title: Finland Sees Continued Demand for Icebreakers Despite Warming Winters, Citing Security Concerns
items.summary: The Finnish multipurpose icebreaker Nordica will support the Canadian Coast Guard under a one-year charter, providing icebreaking, search and rescue, ice management, and environmental response services in the Canadian Arctic. (Credit: Arctia) Finland expects to operate at least as many icebreakers in the coming decades as it does today, despite rising temperatures and declining average ice coverage in the Baltic Sea. This is the conclusion of a new government-commissioned report that also highlights growing security requirements and changes in the commercial shipping fleet. The report warns that the gap between a vessel’s theoretical ice classification and its actual operational capability is becoming more pronounced, potentially increasing demand for icebreaker assistance even as average ice conditions become milder. The first priority is the 1970s-built Urho and Sisu , followed by Kontio and Otso in the 2030s and the multipurpose icebreakers Fennica and Nordica in the 2040s. Finland relies heavily on maritime transport, with more than 95% of its foreign trade in goods carried by sea. The report says reliable winter navigation is essential not only for industrial supply chains and security of supply but also for military mobility. The agencies propose further work on the legal and procurement arrangements by the end of 2026.

items.title: Calmer waters for container spot rates, but ‘fragile’ Middle East a threat
items.original_title: Calmer waters for container spot rates, but ‘fragile’ Middle East a threat
items.summary: There was a certain sense of calm about the container spot freight rate market this week, with slight declines on both the transpacific and Asia-Europe trades as capacity constraints eased and demand remained seasonally subdued. Drewry’s World Container Index (WCI) recorded a 2% week-on-week drop on its Shanghai-Rotterdam leg, to end at $3,615 per 40ft, while the Shanghai-Genoa was flat at $4,166 per 40ft, which indicated that new FAK (freight all kinds) levels, introduced by carriers on 1 November, were unable to stick. The carriers had aimed to push the Asia-North Europe spot rate up to around $4,500 per 40ft and to around $5,000 on Mediterranean shipments. A further attempt at higher FAK levels, around the same as before, is scheduled for 15 November, but modest demand and ample capacity is likely to weigh against them, European forwarders told The Loadstar . “On Asia-Europe rates, we did have initial rates for the fist half of November extended from mid-October, but these are starting to drop a little – I suppose, with the early Chinese New Year, carriers are expecting a small peak, but bookings at this stage would suggest it will not be like previous years,” one said.

items.title: ‘Carrier selection matters’ when it comes to getting your goods on time
items.original_title: ‘Carrier selection matters’ when it comes to getting your goods on time
items.summary: The Asia-North America tradelane is facing the highest ocean freight disruption risk over the coming weeks. Reduced carrier capacity and growing difficulty securing bookings threaten shipment reliability, according to WiseTech Global. The company’s November Ocean Freight Risk Outlook, released today covering weeks 45-48, rates the Asia-North America and Asia-Europe trades as high-risk overall, with Europe-North America assessed as medium risk. It explains that on the transpacific, planned carrier capacity is expected to tighten in the second half of November, driven by reduced supply rather than stronger demand. Booking security risk is also expected to climb to 71% by week 48, well above its historical average of 41%, suggesting growing difficulty securing space on preferred sailings. The latest weekly performance was just 6.5% on time, while 39.1% of arrivals saw delays of eight days or more. Shipment transit time reliability also fell across both Asian tradelanes in October, reaching 21% on Asia-North America, down six percentage points month on month, and 35% on Asia-Europe, a five-point decline. However, on-time performance fell from 39.2% in September to 34.8% in October, while the latest weekly result dropped to 24.6%. Transit-time reliability also weakened, falling three percentage points to 46%.

items.title: Cargo crime in North America down in Q3, but losses are mounting
items.original_title: Cargo crime in North America down in Q3, but losses are mounting
items.summary: Organised criminal networks are increasingly exploiting identity fraud, carrier impersonation and weaknesses in freight verification, driving cargo theft losses across Canada and the US up 39% year on year, despite a sharp decline in reported incidents Verisk CargoNet recorded 2,072 of reported supply chain crime incidents across the countries through to 23 October, marking a 25% decrease in total numbers from the 2,755 recorded during the comparable period in 2025. VP operations at Verisk CargoNet Keith Lewis told The Loadstar : “But while the number of incidents declined, the financial impact moved in the opposite direction, losses increasing 39% to $718.9m.” Furthermore, he noted that the average documented value of stolen goods had also registered a massive surge, 72% year on year, from approximately $261,000 to more than $448,000. Over the third quarter, CargoNet recorded 547 incidents, approximately 33% fewer than a year earlier, but estimated losses still reached $230.1m, with California accounting for the largest share, with 182 incidents, followed by New Jersey, Texas, and Illinois. Among the biggest concerns are fictitious pickups, where criminals impersonate legitimate carriers to collect and divert shipments, with CargoNet recording 138 such incidents in Q3, compared with 147 over the same period of 2025.

items.title: Hong Kong reviews river fees as mainland ports lure cargo away
items.original_title: Hong Kong reviews river fees as mainland ports lure cargo away
items.summary: Hong Kong is reviewing permit fees charged to river trade vessels as it seeks to maintain its port’s competitiveness amid growing competition from mainland Chinese terminals in Guangzhou and Shenzhen. The secretary for transport and logistics, Chan Mei-po, announced the review in a written reply to the Legislative Council on Wednesday. China-flagged vessels carry containers between ports in the Pearl River Delta and Hong Kong, where cargo may be transferred to ocean-going vessels for onward shipment. Hong Kong operates a multiple-entry permit scheme, allowing operators to make up to 10 port entries within a month for a fee equivalent to five single-entries – the “buy five, get five free” system. Ms Chan said: “The Action Plan on Maritime and Port Development Strategy proposes various measures to strengthen Hong Kong’s position as a regional transhipment hub, including reviewing the permit fees charged to river trade vessels in order to maintain the competitiveness and attractiveness of the port to the industry. We have completed a preliminary review and are now discussing the matter with relevant departments, with the details to be released in due course.” Laden container movements between Hong Kong and mainland China account for more than 40% of the territory’s annual laden container throughput.

items.summary: Thailand’s Precious Shipping is preparing a change at the top, with longtime managing director Khalid Moinuddin Hashim moving to executive vice chairman and finance chief Gautam Khurana taking over the running of the Bangkok-listed dry bulk owner. The company’s board approved the leadership reshuffle, with both appointments taking effect on January 1, 2027, according to a filing with the Stock Exchange of Thailand. Khurana will continue to serve as director of finance until a successor is appointed. The transition marks a significant shift for Precious Shipping, which has been led by Hashim for more than three decades. The management shake-up comes amid a major fleet renewal programme that has seen Precious sell ageing handysize and supramax vessels while expanding its ultramax fleet. In September, the company returned to China’s Taizhou Sanfu Ship Engineering for four 64,500 dwt ultramax newbuildings worth a combined $141.8m, with deliveries scheduled between April 2030 and January 2031. The order followed an earlier $133.46m contract for four 63,500 dwt ultramaxes at the same yard, with two vessels already in service and the remaining pair due through the first quarter of 2027. Once the outstanding newbuildings arrive, Precious expects its fleet to reach 47 vessels totalling about 2.34m dwt.

According to the International Transport Workers’ Federation, many crews face severe shortages of food, drinking water, fuel, medical assistance, and unpaid wages, while more than 40 sailors have reportedly been killed. items.summary: The Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore (MPA), the Research Council of Norway (RCN) and the Singapore Maritime Institute (SMI) have launched a joint research grant call to develop solutions to support the decarbonisation of international shipping. The joint grant call brings together the research, technology and industry capabilities of Singapore’s and Norway’s maritime innovation ecosystems to address shared technological and operational challenges and develop solutions applicable across international shipping. The grant call builds on the MPA-RCN Memorandum of Understanding signed in April 2024 on maritime research, development, education and training. The grant call will focus on three areas: · Alternative fuels and energy infrastructure: Improving the safety and handling of alternative marine fuels, developing bunkering and fuel storage technologies, and advancing charging infrastructure for electric vessels. · Digitalisation and greener shipping operations: Advancing voyage optimisation, just-in-time arrivals, autonomous operations and ship-port data exchange to improve operational efficiency and reduce emissions. SMI will provide up to S$2.7 million for Singapore research partners, while RCN will make available up to NOK 20 million for Norwegian research partners. Each proposal must involve research institutions and industry partners from both countries to ensure that the research addresses practical industry needs.

items.original_title: Kalé Research Identifies That Only Five Per Cent Of Ports Are Fully Digitised
items.summary: Only five percent of respondents said a Port Community System (PCS) was fully implemented at their port, according to new global research from Kalé Logistics (Kalé). Launched at the International Association of Ports and Harbors World Ports Conference, the State of Port Digital Readiness & Stakeholder Adoption of Port Community Systems report found half of respondents identified customs as the primary barrier to adoption, while 35 per cent cited other government agencies. “Ports are facing greater supply chain disruption, congestion, labour volatility, and compliance demands, but technology alone cannot solve these pressures while information remains fragmented between organisations and regulatory systems,” said Vineet Malhotra, Co-Founder and Director, Kalé. “The next phase of port digitalisation requires policy, people, and technology to move together, with authorities enabling trusted data exchange and ensuring developing markets are not left behind.” PCS connect public and private organisations across a port through a shared digital environment, allowing data to be securely exchanged and reused to reduce paperwork, congestion, delays, and duplicated processes, while improving cargo visibility and coordination. It finds 79 per cent of respondents report that their port does not have a fully operational PCS, while 22 per cent highlighted digital skills gaps as a barrier to adoption, and uptake remains particularly weak in low-income countries.

items.title: Advancing maritime digitalization in West and Central Africa
items.original_title: Advancing maritime digitalization in West and Central Africa
items.summary: The digitalization of ports across nine West and Central African countries has been boosted through a regional workshop in Accra, Ghana. The event was organized by IMO, the Africa Transport Policy Program (SSATP), and the World Bank, in partnership with the Ghana Maritime Authority. The key aims of the event included: • Promoting the adoption of the IMO Compendium on Facilitation and Electronic Business, which sets out how shipping and port data are structured and shared electronically to streamline communication; and • Scaling up the implementation of Maritime Single Windows (MSWs) and Port Community Systems (PCSs), which are integrated digital platforms that streamline vessel and cargo clearance, reduce bureaucratic delays, and will help to strengthen Africa’s competitiveness in global maritime trade. Promoting regional collaboration The workshop convened regional and international institutions committed to translating policy into action, including the Port Management Association of West and Central Africa (PMAWCA), the African Development Bank (AfDB), the African Harbour Masters’ Committee (AHMC), and the African Alliance for Electronic Commerce (AAEC). The workshop was structured around both knowledge sharing and practical capacity building, with 55 participants, including 15 women, from maritime administrations, port authorities, and customs authorities in Cabo Verde, Equatorial Guinea, The Gambia, Ghana, Guinea-Bissau, Liberia, Nigeria, São Tomé and Príncipe, and Sierra Leone.

items.summary: Swedish industrial group Alfa Laval has struck a $700m all-cash deal to acquire Norwegian maritime software specialist NAVTOR, significantly expanding a digital shipping portfolio that already includes StormGeo and Portchain. The Stockholm-listed group has entered into a definitive agreement to buy NAVTOR for SEK6.85bn ($700m), with completion expected during the first quarter of 2027 subject to regulatory approvals. Alfa Laval described the purchase as one of the most significant transactions in its history. Alfa Laval said it expects the business to generate about $194m in revenue this year. “With this acquisition, Alfa Laval will expand its digital offering at a time when real-time decision-making is increasingly complex,” said chief executive Tom Erixon. US technology investor Accel-KKR took a majority stake in NAVTOR in 2020, followed by purchases of performance analytics specialist Tres Solutions in 2021 and digital logbook developer Ingenium Marine in 2022. NAVTOR then combined with Voyager Worldwide in 2023, creating a business whose technology at the time served about 18,000 vessels. Alfa Laval has been assembling its own maritime software stack since buying weather routing and voyage optimisation company StormGeo for NOK3.63bn in 2021. Alfa Laval also disclosed that a recent NAVTOR internal review identified unspecified compliance matters, prompting the Norwegian company to strengthen its internal controls and compliance programme.

items.title: Indian ship recycling breakthrough hits Brussels roadblock
items.original_title: Indian ship recycling breakthrough hits Brussels roadblock
items.summary: A European Parliament committee has voted against allowing two Indian shipbreaking yards onto the EU’s approved recycling list, dealing a setback to shipowners pushing for greater access to South Asian dismantling capacity. The Parliament’s environment committee backed an objection this week to the European Commission’s proposal to approve Shree Ram Vessel Scrap and YSI Recyclers, both located in the Alang-Sosiya shipbreaking hub in Gujarat. The two facilities had received preliminary backing from the Commission following inspections intended to establish whether they met the requirements of the EU Ship Recycling Regulation. Their inclusion would make them the first facilities on the Indian subcontinent to join the European list. Environmental organisations and recycling industry representatives have taken the opposite position, arguing that beaching operations cannot provide sufficient containment of hazardous materials and should not qualify for EU recognition. Campaigners have also challenged the industry’s argument that additional capacity is needed, pointing to more than 2m light displacement tonnes of combined annual capacity at facilities already on the EU list, which they claim is sufficient to handle recent recycling volumes involving EU-flagged and EU-owned ships. Under EU rules, EU-flagged commercial ships subject to the Ship Recycling Regulation must be dismantled at facilities on the approved European list.

items.title: Shipping has a coffee problem
items.original_title: Shipping has a coffee problem
items.summary: From Posidonia to Geneva Dry, the shipping industry’s favourite pastime appears to be arranging coffee meetings that may or may not actually happen. Mike Darby from Merchant Recruitment makes the case for the Baltic Flat White Index. In bunkering, the cappuccino effect means paying for froth instead of fuel. I’m increasingly convinced that approximately 70% of the shipping industry is trying to arrange a coffee with the other 30%. Then there’s the person who manages to arrange eight coffee meetings between 9am and midday. An impressive achievement considering each meeting is apparently going to last 30 minutes, nobody knows where they’re meeting and the exhibition centre is roughly the size of a small European country. By 4pm, the original coffee meeting has somehow turned into drinks, dinner and a discussion about whether anyone actually knows who’s paying. Then there’s the classic closing line: ”We must do this more often.” Which, translated into shipping language, means we’ll probably bump into each other in Athens next June, promise to arrange another coffee and repeat the entire process. Shipping remains a relationship-driven industry, and despite all the technology, digitalisation and virtual meetings, there’s still something valuable about sitting down with someone face-to-face.

items.original_title: Seven Shadow Fleet Tankers Spoof AIS to Hide Novorossiysk Voyages
items.summary: Sanctioned Tankers Fake Their Positions Near the Bosphorus A cluster of seven sanctioned Russian tankers were found to have routinely and deliberately manipulated AIS over the past 90 days to falsely claim they were drifting off the Black Sea close to the Bosphorus entrance. The tankers were instead identified by Windward clandestinely sailing for the Russian oil terminal of Novorossiysk to load oil, hugging the Black Sea coastline to try and avoid Ukrainian drone attacks. At the same time, the tankers manipulated their AIS, a process known as spoofing. Windward Identifies Seven Sanctioned Shadow Fleet Tankers The vessels identified were a Sierra Leone-flagged Suezmax tanker, a Russia-flagged Aframax, a Russia-flagged Aframax tanker, an Equatorial Guinea-flagged Suezmax, an Equatorial Guinea-flagged Aframax, a Comoros-flagged Suezmax, and a Russia-flagged Aframax tanker. All are sanctioned, shadow fleet vessels. Periods of GNSS manipulation lasted around 2-3 weeks, the duration for tankers to sail to Novorossiysk, load, and return. While many vessels are switching off their AIS for legitimate safety and security reasons in the Black Sea, Russian shadow fleet tankers are using deceptive shipping practices, including GNSS manipulation, to avoid targeting by Ukrainian drones. A further seven cargo ships were damaged in attacks attributed to Russia off Bulgaria and Romania just outside their territorial waters over October.

Complementing this unique dataset is a series of interviews with maritime safety experts conducted by Inmarsat’s research partner, SeaFocus International, as part of the Safety Hub’s development. Managing weather hazards Among the 106,975 maritime safety broadcasts made in 2025, 2.6% were marked ‘urgent’. Having access to more granular data on a vessel’s vulnerability to extreme weather can therefore help crew avoid distress situations. Persistent challenges, evolving risks While Inmarsat received fewer GMDSS calls in 2025 (741) than in 2023 (788) and 2024 (801), the three-year trend remains broadly consistent with historical averages, reflecting how established safety challenges persist even as new risks emerge. items.title: Greenland’s scrubber ban sparks calls for wider Arctic crackdown
items.original_title: Greenland’s scrubber ban sparks calls for wider Arctic crackdown
items.summary: Greenland is moving to ban scrubber wastewater discharges throughout its territorial waters, prompting environmental groups to call for similar restrictions across the Arctic and ultimately a global prohibition. The country’s parliament, Inatsisartut, voted unanimously last month to direct the government to introduce a phased ban covering ports, internal waters and territorial seas extending 12 nautical miles offshore. Discharges from open-loop scrubbers will be prohibited from July 1, 2027, followed by closed-loop and hybrid systems from July 1, 2029. The restrictions will require affected ships to switch to compliant fuels or retain scrubber wastewater onboard while operating in Greenlandic waters. “The decision by Greenland’s parliament to ban scrubber discharges is an important step towards cleaner shipping, and a clear signal for other countries to do the same,” said Kaare Press-Kristensen, senior advisor at Green Global Future. Sian Prior, lead advisor to the Clean Arctic Alliance, is urging the IMO to introduce a global ban, starting with the environmentally sensitive Arctic. Greenland’s decision follows Denmark’s prohibition on open-loop discharges in July 2025, with Sweden and Finland introducing similar measures. The move also goes beyond the 2025 OSPAR agreement, which mandates phased restrictions in ports and internal waters but currently only recommends extending them to territorial seas.

items.title: China’s property starts plunge to 2002 levels
items.original_title: China’s property starts plunge to 2002 levels
items.summary: China’s property construction collapse has taken new building starts back to levels last seen in 2002, raising fresh questions about the long-term outlook for iron ore and coking coal demand, even as dry bulk owners become increasingly bullish about freight markets. Research published today by Ursa Shipbrokers reveals that Chinese property starts have fallen by 74% since 2019, from 2.27bn sq m to just 588m sq m last year. The deterioration is continuing. In the first nine months of 2026, new starts totalled 340m sq m, down 25% year-on-year and almost 80% below the equivalent period in 2019. Ursa notes that although construction starts have returned to levels comparable with the early 2000s, the circumstances could scarcely be more different. Chinese iron ore imports actually increased 4.1% in the first nine months of 2026, reflecting greater reliance on overseas supplies, inventory accumulation and changing trade patterns. Dionysios Tsilioris, a researcher with Ursa, told Splash today that the historic link between Chinese property starts and capesize earnings has disconnected to a large degree. China’s traditional construction-led demand engine continues to deteriorate, but longer trading distances and shifting mineral supply chains are helping support freight markets. Whether those factors can continue offsetting China’s structural property slump is emerging as a central question for capesize owners.

One Captain describes manageable workloads at sea, followed by cargo operations, inspections, regulatory requirements and paperwork converging in port, while the office presses for shorter turnarounds. The Seafarers Happiness Index describes extraordinary commitment, but that should not be allowed to reassure us too much. A system can appear successful precisely because the people within it are absorbing its failures. We cannot keep demanding more from less and assuming resilience will fill the gaps.

items.title: Hormuz Oct crossings at 3-month high despite attacks, Red Sea traffic also rises
items.original_title: Hormuz Oct crossings at 3-month high despite attacks, Red Sea traffic also rises
items.summary: Strait of Hormuz shipping traffic rose to its highest monthly level since July in October, supported by stronger dry-bulk and LNG movements despite a decline in VLCC traffic and mounting regional threats, S&P Global Commodities at Sea(opens in a new tab) data showed Nov. 2. The rise came amid an “increasingly volatile” operating environment at Hormuz and the Bab al-Mandab Strait, with “reported projectile strikes, vessel fires and other security incidents” throughout October, CAS said. Despite elevated security risks over the month, observed and assumed Hormuz traffic totaled 750 transits in October, up from 749 in September, as VLCC traffic fell to 156 transits in October from 184 the previous month, but the declines in crude tanker transits were more than offset by other vessel classes, according to the CAS report. LNG carrier crossings, which fell steeply since Qatar LNG production units suffered damage at the start of the Iran war, also climbed, reaching 32 transits, or their highest since the start of the war. The Iranian authority had listed 240 vessels as violating its Strait of Hormuz transit guidelines and previously threatened non-compliant vessels with fines, seizure or confiscation. In the Red Sea, Bab al-Mandab traffic rose to 1,196 transits in October from 1,154 in September, while tanker movements were stable at 408 versus 404, CAS reported.

items.title: Alternative fuels need infrastructure: Why gas bunker vessels matter
items.original_title: Alternative fuels need infrastructure: Why gas bunker vessels matter
items.summary: The maritime industry is entering a period of growing fuel diversity. While much of the discussion focuses on fuels, engines, and regulations, the transition will also depend on the infrastructure needed to supply alternative fuels safely, reliably, and at scale. DNV’s new white paper, Gas bunker vessels – Facilitating the transition to alternative fuels, details how gas bunker vessels are becoming a critical part of that infrastructure and analyses the key factors shaping their future development, from market growth and vessel design to safety, operational readiness, and the adoption of emerging fuels such as ammonia. According to DNV’s Alternative Fuels Insight platform, around 900 LNG-fuelled vessels are now in operation worldwide, excluding LNG carriers. “Our analysis suggests the global LNG bunker vessel fleet may need to more than double by 2030, with between 165 and 208 vessels potentially required worldwide. Meeting that demand will require coordinated investment across the entire bunkering value chain, not just in the vessels themselves.” Gas bunker vessels emerge as a key link in the alternative fuel value chain The report argues that gas bunker vessels should be viewed as more than fuel delivery assets. While gas bunker vessels share many characteristics with conventional gas carriers, their role as fuel suppliers creates a distinct operating profile.

items.title: Chinese Penetrate South Korea’s LNG Carrier Market
items.original_title: Chinese Penetrate South Korea’s LNG Carrier Market
items.summary: Chinese shipbuilders secured approximately 40% of all newly ordered large liquefied natural gas (LNG) carriers worldwide during the first to third quarters of this year, January to September. While China leads in the general merchant ship market, such as container ships and bulk carriers, by leveraging price competitiveness, large high-value-added LNG carriers with a capacity of 174,000 cubic meters or more were considered a market dominated by South Korean shipbuilders, who possess differentiated technology. Chinese shipyards have aggressively penetrated this sector this year. However, Chinese shipyards have recently entered the LNG carrier market one after another, beginning to accumulate experience and engaging in a “long-term battle.” Until 2021, only Hudong-Zhonghua Shipbuilding in China could construct large LNG carriers. As the first Chinese company to build and deliver a large LNG carrier in 2008, it grew by securing 36 orders out of 128 LNG carriers ordered by Qatar during its mass LNG production drive from 2020 to 2024, excluding those secured by South Korean shipyards. Over the past four years, four additional Chinese shipyards—Jiangnan Shipyard, Dalian Shipbuilding Industry, Yangzijiang Shipyard, and China Merchants—have entered the LNG carrier market. Jiangnan Shipyard delivered its first 175,000 cubic meter-class LNG carrier to a shipowner in November 2024, while Dalian Shipyard did so in September of last year, already accumulating shipbuilding experience.

items.summary: Between October 29 and 30, Iran attacked at least four tankers across the Strait of Hormuz and the waters around it. Iranian sources separately claimed that four tankers hit mines in the Strait and caught fire, but it is unclear whether they were referring to additional vessels beyond the four confirmed. Projectiles Strike a Laden LNG Carrier Inside the Gulf On October 30, AL MAYEDA (IMO 9397298), a Marshall Islands-flagged, Qatari-owned LNG carrier, laden with an unknown quantity of LNG according to Vortexa, was struck by three projectiles around 18:00 UTC, approximately 40 nautical miles south of Lavan Island. AL MAYEDA had previously been dark between September 27 and October 30, and crossed inbound through the Strait of Hormuz during that period. Limpet Mines Return to the Gulf The same day, a small boat approached LOUISE 1 (IMO 9290323), a Panama-flagged, Panama-owned crude oil tanker, approximately 25 nautical miles northeast of Khasab, Oman, and emplaced two explosive devices on its hull. Why the Return of Limpet Mines Matters This latest round of attacks continues the trend established this month while expanding the methods Iran is using.

items.title: Japan Revives Shipbuilding with New LNG Dock
items.original_title: Japan Revives Shipbuilding with New LNG Dock
items.summary: Japan has embarked on a full-scale revival of its shipbuilding industry. To resume the construction of liquefied natural gas (LNG) carriers, the country is establishing a new large-scale dock for the first time in 18 years, and it is reactivating halted shipbuilding lines in response to defense budget increases and naval vessel export expansion. The prospect is that cooperation and competition between the shipbuilding industries of South Korea and Japan will intertwine, as Japan seeks technological cooperation with South Korean shipbuilders on LNG carriers while simultaneously emerging as a competitor in naval vessel exports. According to Japanese media such as the Nihon Keizai Shimbun and the Asahi Shimbun, Namura Shipbuilding will construct a new large-scale dock capable of building LNG carriers and other vessels in Imari Bay, Saga Prefecture by 2035. This marks the first time a new dock for large vessels has been built in Japan since Imabari Shipbuilding’s Marugame Headquarters in 2017. The Imari Works already possesses a large dock measuring about 450 meters in length and about 70 meters in width, but the company determined that additional production capacity is necessary as high utilization rates continue due to increased shipbuilding demand.

items.summary: Technology group Wärtsilä has successfully completed the conversion of one engine on three LNG carriers operated by Chevron Transport Corporation from dual-fuel (DF) to spark gas (SG) operation. This conversion aims to lower greenhouse gas emissions from the vessels by reducing methane slip, un-combusted methane that can escape into the atmosphere from LNG fuel. Following the successful conversion of these first three vessels, three additional vessel conversions are planned for execution later this year and next year, bringing the total number of converted vessels to six. This project represents a technical collaboration within the marine sector focused on addressing methane emissions from LNG-fueled vessels. Wärtsilä has successfully completed the conversion of one engine on three LNG carriers operated by Chevron Transport Corporation from dual-fuel (DF) to spark gas (SG) operation. © Chevron Shipping The Spark Gas Conversion for the Wärtsilä 50DF engine minimises methane emissions by introducing an electrically controlled pre-combustion chamber valve. The estimated result is that, on an IMO weighted (E2-cycle) average, the conversion reduces methane emissions down to 1.1 percent of fuel use. The solution is available to vessels in the industry with existing Wärtsilä 50DF engines for diesel-electric propulsion, the majority of which are LNG carriers.

items.title: Poland has EU’s second-highest electricity prices accounting for cost of living
items.original_title: Poland has EU’s second-highest electricity prices accounting for cost of living
items.summary: Poland had the second-highest household electricity prices in the European Union in the first half of 2026 after adjusting for differences in the cost of living, new Eurostat data show. In nominal terms, Polish households paid €29.99 per 100 kilowatt-hours (kWh) for electricity in the first half of 2026. However, when adjusted for purchasing power standards (PPS), which account for differences in the cost of living, Poland ranked second in the EU, at 41.12 PPS per 100 kWh. One reason why electricity prices in Poland remain high is the country’s continued reliance on coal, which last year generated just over half of power , by far the highest proportion in the EU. These costs contribute to the high taxes and levies included in household electricity bills, which accounted for 39% of the final price in Poland in the first half of 2026. Without taxes and levies, the nominal price of electricity in Poland would have been just under €16 per 100 kWh, below the EU average of €20.27.

items.summary: Union Pacific led the way on the North American containerised rail freight front over the three months to October, amid all the noise surrounding its pending acquisition of Norfolk Southern – but it was not alone in enjoying a bountiful summer. In general, North American intermodal operators benefited from an upswing in domestic freight demand and a continuing tightening in the trucking market, with revenues up for all four of the major carriers. Boasting a 27% year-on-year revenue increase, Union Pacific took home some $1.52bn over the quarter, with volumes up 11%, to 956,000 carloads, and pointing specifically to reduced trucking capacity as behind the gains. “We’re very optimistic about the opportunities as we close this year and go into next on the domestic intermodal side,” she told investors, adding that the tightening in trucking could prove a boost when yields come up for renewal. Not one to miss out, Canadian Pacific Kansas City (CPKC) also reported double-digit revenue growth in intermodal, up 22% year on year to $583m, as volumes rose 9%, to 489,800 carloads. Together with the increased traffic, stronger pricing likely played its part in driving the improvement for the Canadian operator that saw its revenue per carload increase 12% year on year, to $1,190.

items.title: Norway Detains Sanctioned Chinese Vessel Over False Flag Registration
items.original_title: Norway Detains Sanctioned Chinese Vessel Over False Flag Registration
items.summary: Norway has detained a Chinese-owned heavy-lift vessel sanctioned for its role in delivering equipment to Russia’s Arctic LNG 2 project, in what appears to be the first known detention in the Arctic of a Chinese vessel linked to Russia’s shadow fleet. The Ya Qing Hai Yang was detained after Norwegian inspectors found that it lacked valid flag-state registration and required certificates, the Norwegian Maritime Authority said. The case is a notable enforcement action against a vessel with documented ties to Russia’s sanctioned energy sector, although authorities say the detention was based on maritime safety and registration deficiencies rather than the ship’s sanctions status. “During the inspection, it was discovered that the vessel did not have a valid flag registration and lacked the required certificates,” Dag Inge Aarhus, the authority’s communications director said last week. “The vessel has therefore been detained until further notice.” The vessel remains off the Vesterålen Islands as of November 3. The ship must establish valid registration with a flag state and obtain the necessary certificates before Norwegian authorities can complete the inspection and consider its release. The detention appears to be the first publicly documented case of Norway holding a vessel sailing under an invalid flag registration. The United States sanctioned the vessel’s operator and related entities in January 2025 .

items.original_title: Offshore operators should not wait for EU ETS clarity to act on emissions data
items.summary: EU MRV has applied to offshore vessels of 400 GT and above since 1 January 2025, and vessels of 5,000 GT and above are scheduled to enter the EU ETS from the 2027 reporting period. On 17 July 2026, the European Commission published proposals that would revise the MRV framework from 1 January 2029 and bring offshore vessels between 400 and 5,000 GT into the ETS from 2031. These are not final, however, and must still pass through the legislative process. The International Marine Contractors Association (IMCA) has welcomed the recognition of offshore-specific terminology and operational realities, but says more clarity is needed on ports of call, cross-border operations and how the EU and UK ETS interact. In August, Norway’s Ministry of Climate and Environment confirmed that FuelEU Maritime and ReFuelEU Aviation, previously expected to take effect later this year, will not enter into force for Norway before 1 January 2028. From 2029, companies operating on the Norwegian continental shelf must reduce the greenhouse gas intensity of ships used in oil and gas activity, starting at 10% for 2029-2031 and rising in stages to 40% for 2038-2040. Rystad Energy estimates close to 300 offshore vessels fall within scope, and that most of them, including LNG dual-fuel units, would miss the first threshold based on how they operate today.

items.title: Singapore VLSFO back above $1,000 for first time since March
items.original_title: Singapore VLSFO back above $1,000 for first time since March
items.summary: The cost of fuelling ships has climbed back above $1,000 a tonne in Singapore for the first time since March, as the prolonged Iran conflict continues to drive up bunker bills across the global merchant fleet. Data from Ship & Bunker show very low sulphur fuel oil (VLSFO) broke through the $1,000 threshold on October 28, reaching $1,000.50 a tonne. Prices subsequently climbed to $1,019.50 on Friday before easing to $1,003.50 on Monday. Ship & Bunker data show Singapore VLSFO was trading at $521.50 a tonne immediately before the conflict. The fuel has since increased by more than 92%, having reached a peak of $1,120.50 on March 13. For a ship taking on 3,000 tonnes of VLSFO, the current bunker bill is approximately $3m, compared with $1.56m before the war, an additional $1.45m for a single stem. Scrubber-equipped vessels retain a significant advantage, with the Singapore VLSFO-HSFO spread currently standing at $105 a tonne. According to bunker pricing specialist ENGINE, LNG bunkers in Singapore reached $1,939 a tonne on Monday, up $74 over the previous week. Ship & Bunker assessed Rotterdam VLSFO at $763.50 a tonne on Monday, around $240 below Singapore, while Fujairah was quoted at $991.50.
